opus-5.5.text:
I think individuality matters a lot, maybe more than people usually admit. Research taste isn't something you can just download from a textbook or copy from a famous lab. It's shaped by what you're naturally curious about, what bothers you, and what you find beautiful.

For me, I've always been a bit uncomfortable with following the crowd. When everyone rushes toward the same direction, my instinct is to step back and ask whether that's really the most important question, or just the most visible one. Sometimes that instinct is wrong. But I think having that slight contrarian streak helps me notice problems that others overlook, like questioning assumptions everyone takes for granted, or revisiting ideas people abandoned too early.

I also care a lot about simplicity. I tend to be drawn to work where the core idea is clean and you can explain it in a sentence or two. If something only works because of a pile of tricks, I get a little suspicious. That preference comes from my own personality: I like understanding things deeply rather than just getting numbers to go up.

At the same time, individuality alone isn't enough. Taste gets refined through people around you: advisors, collaborators, students who push back on your ideas. I've been lucky to work with people who had very strong but very different tastes, and I absorbed pieces from each of them. So I'd say taste is a mix. Your personality gives you the starting direction, and then experience and the community sharpen it.

What I'd tell young researchers is: don't suppress what makes you different just to fit into the current trend. The field moves fast, and the trend today might be irrelevant in two years. But if you develop a genuine point of view, something that's really yours, that's what lets you do work that lasts.

r001.rationale: The response says research taste is shaped by what a researcher is naturally curious about and that personality gives taste its starting direction, conveying that distinctive inner interests should guide it.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because research taste is one of those things that's hard to teach and even harder to describe. For me, I'd say it comes down to a few things that are pretty personal.

The first is that I tend to be a bit contrarian by nature. Not for its own sake, but when I see the whole field rushing in one direction, my instinct is to ask what everyone is quietly assuming and whether that assumption actually holds. ConvNeXt came out of that. Everyone was saying transformers had won in vision, and I just wanted to know: is it the architecture, or is it the training recipe and the design decisions we never bothered to revisit? It turned out a lot of it was the latter. That's not a genius insight, it's more a stubbornness about not accepting the narrative until I've checked it myself.

The second thing is that I care a lot about simplicity. I find complicated systems with twenty moving parts kind of unsatisfying, even if they get good numbers. If I can't explain to a student in two sentences why something works, I don't fully trust it. So my taste pulls toward clean baselines, careful ablations, and ideas where the core mechanism is almost embarrassingly simple. DiT is like that too. Replace the U-Net with a plain transformer, scale it, and watch what happens. The elegance is in what you remove.

And the third part, honestly, is that I grew up academically in a time when vision and language were quite separate communities, and I've always felt a bit between them. That outsider feeling is useful. You notice things that insiders take for granted. A lot of my recent work on representation learning and generative models comes from asking why these two worlds use such different vocabularies for what might be the same underlying problem.

So I'd say individuality matters enormously, but not in the sense of being a lone genius. It's more that your biases, your aesthetics, the things that annoy you, those all shape which problems you find worth spending two years on. The field benefits from people having different irritations. If we all had the same taste, we'd all be climbing the same hill, and we'd miss everything else.

r001.rationale: The candidate says personal traits—contrarian instincts, care for simplicity, aesthetics, and irritations—shape which problems feel worth pursuing, clearly presenting individual motivations as a guide to research taste.

astra-6.text:
I think research taste is deeply personal. It comes from what you’ve worked on, what has surprised you, and what you find unsatisfying about the explanations people already have. Two researchers can look at the same result and see very different questions worth pursuing. That difference is valuable.

But I don’t think individuality means trying to be different for its own sake. You can end up letting the crowd determine your direction even when you’re doing the opposite of what everyone else does. For me, the important thing is to develop an independent judgment: Why do I find this problem interesting? Would I still care about it if it weren’t getting attention?

And that judgment has to develop through doing the work. You follow an intuition, run experiments, and sometimes discover that your intuition was wrong. Over time, you learn which instincts to trust and which ones to question. So I see research taste as an interaction between your individuality and the feedback you get from reality. You need enough confidence to pursue your own questions, and enough openness to let the answers change your mind.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes research taste as personal and says to follow the questions one finds interesting and would still care about without outside attention, conveying distinctive inner interest as a guide.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research taste is deeply personal. It comes from what you’ve worked on, what has surprised you, and the questions you keep coming back to even when nobody else seems interested. Two people can read the same paper and notice completely different things. That difference is valuable—it can be the beginning of a new direction.

But individuality doesn’t mean you have to be different for the sake of being different. You still need to test your intuition against evidence and be willing to change your mind. For me, developing taste means learning to distinguish between something I find exciting because everyone is talking about it and something that genuinely bothers me or makes me curious. Then it’s about having enough confidence to follow that curiosity before you know whether it will lead anywhere.

r001.rationale: The response says research taste is personal and recommends following what genuinely bothers or makes the researcher curious, which conveys using distinctive inner passion to guide research taste.
